function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It will:

1. Clone the repo.  
2. Inspect the repo (you’ll see a very small Node.js “Hello World” app).  
3. Create a production‑ready Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow.  
4. Stage, commit, and push the changes back to the remote.

> **NOTE** – All commands assume you’re running them from a Unix‑like shell (Linux/macOS).  
> If you’re on Windows, use PowerShell or Git‑Bash.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH access, replace the URL with the HTTPS clone URL:
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a minimal `app.js` that listens on port `3000`.  
We’ll build a lightweight image using `node:18-alpine`.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣ Base image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# 2️⃣ Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# 3️⃣ Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 4️⃣ Copy source code
COPY . .

# 5️⃣ Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 6️⃣ Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the repo root.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes manifests

Create a `k8s/` directory and add two files: `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update after CI builds
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Tip** – If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `ci.yml`.

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

#### `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (optional, but useful for pushing images)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # (Optional) Deploy to a cluster – uncomment if you have a kubeconfig secret
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      #   with:
      #     manifests: |
      #       k8s/deployment.yaml
      #       k8s/service.yaml
      #     images: |
      #       ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Builds the image on every push to `main`.  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * The image tag `latest` will be used by the Kubernetes manifests.  
> * The SHA‑based tag (`${{ github.sha }}`) is useful for rollbacks.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage all new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

1. **GitHub Actions** – Go to the *Actions* tab of the repo; you should see a successful run.  
2. **Docker image** – Check `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome` for the `latest` tag.  
3. **Kubernetes** – If you have a cluster configured, apply the manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

> The deployment will pull the image from GHCR and expose it via the service.

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A production‑ready Dockerfile for a Node.js app.  
- Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs.  
- A GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main`.  

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image registry, or add more environment variables as your project grows. Happy coding!
